            "A point extends into a one-dimensional line.",

        self.play(

        # 1D line representation
        line_1d = Line(LEFT, RIGHT, color=YELLOW_C)
        self.place_at_grid(line_1d, "B4", scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(ReplacementTransform(dot, line_1d))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===

        self.play(

    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout(
            "Puzzle 1: The Shortest Path (3D to 2D Shift)",
            [
                "A spider wants the shortest path to a fly.",
                "Navigating a 3D room makes the path look complex.",
                "We can flatten the room into a single 2D plane.",
                "On this flat map, the shortest path is a line.",
                "This 2D shift reveals the hidden hypotenuse path."
            ]

        # Assets
        spider_svg_path = "/mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/spider.svg"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===

        # Room geometry (3D projection)
        front_wall = Square(side_length=1.5, color="#808080", fill_opacity=0.3)
        side_wall = Polygon(
            front_wall.get_corner(UR),
            front_wall.get_corner(UR) + RIGHT * 1 + UP * 0.5,
            front_wall.get_corner(DR) + RIGHT * 1 + UP * 0.5,
            front_wall.get_corner(DR),
            color="#808080", fill_opacity=0.3
        )
        
        room_net_group = VGroup(front_wall, side_wall)
        self.place_in_area(room_net_group, 'B2', 'E5', scale_factor=0.9)
        
        # Spider (SVG) and Fly (Dot)
        spider = SVGMobject(spider_svg_path, color=WHITE).scale(0.15)
        spider.move_to(front_wall.get_corner(DL))
        
        fly = Dot(color=RED, radius=0.08)
        fly.move_to(side_wall.get_vertices()[1]) # Top-right vertex of the side wall
        
        self.lecture[0].set_color(YELLOW)
        self.play(Create(room_net_group), FadeIn(spider), FadeIn(fly), run_time=1.5)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # A dashed pink #FF00FF line shows the spider's path across two walls.
        
        # Intersection point on the shared edge between the two walls
        shared_edge_point = (front_wall.get_corner(UR) + front_wall.get_corner(DR)) / 2 + DOWN * 0.2
        path_seg1 = DashedLine(spider.get_center(), shared_edge_point, color="#FF00FF")
        path_seg2 = DashedLine(shared_edge_point, fly.get_center(), color="#FF00FF")
        complex_path = VGroup(path_seg1, path_seg2)

        spider_target_pos = flat_front.get_corner(DL)
        fly_target_pos = flat_side.get_corner(UR)
        
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        self.play(
            FadeOut(complex_path),
            ReplacementTransform(front_wall, flat_front),
            ReplacementTransform(side_wall, flat_side),
            spider.animate.move_to(spider_target_pos),
            fly.animate.move_to(fly_target_pos),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===

        net_label = Text("Unfolded Net", font_size=20, color="#808080")

        self.lecture[2].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[3].set_color(YELLOW)
        self.play(FadeIn(net_label), run_time=1)
        self.wait(1)

outline.topic: Beyond the Flatland: Solving Geometry Puzzles with Dimensional Shifts
outline.target_audience: High school students and curious learners with a basic understanding of geometry

sections.title: The Boundary Constraint: Why Dimensions Matter
sections.content: Introduction to the concept of 'Dimensional Constraints.' We establish the hook: some problems are impossible to solve within their own dimension. This section introduces 'Flatland' logic where a 2D character is trapped by a simple line.
sections.example: An ant is trapped inside a circle drawn on a piece of paper. To the 2D ant, the circle is an infinite wall. However, a 3D human sees this as a minor hurdle that can be bypassed by simply 'stepping over' it into the third dimension.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: The N+1 Foundation
sections.content: A quick visual primer on dimensions. We define 0D (Point), 1D (Line/X-axis), 2D (Plane/XY-axes), and 3D (Space/XYZ-axes). Crucially, we introduce the concept of a 'Net'—the 2D unfolded skin of a 3D object.
sections.example: Visualizing a cube as it unfolds into a cross-shaped 2D 'net.' This transition shows that the distance between two points on a 3D surface can be measured as a straight line in 2D.

sections.title: Puzzle 1: The Shortest Path (3D to 2D Shift)
sections.content: Solving the 'Spider and the Fly' problem. Instead of navigating 3D space, we flatten the environment into a 2D plane to find the geodesic (the shortest distance). This demonstrates the 'unfolding' technique.
sections.example: A spider at one corner of a rectangular room needs to reach a fly at the opposite corner. By 'unfolding' the walls and ceiling of the room into a single 2D flat map, the spider’s complex 3D path becomes a simple straight line (Hypotenuse).

sections.title: Puzzle 2: The Impossible Knot (2D to 3D Shift)
sections.content: Introducing the concept of 'extruding' a problem. We look at two intertwined rings in 2D that cannot be separated without breaking. By shifting into 3D, we gain a new degree of freedom to resolve the intersection.
sections.example: Imagine two paper-thin rings linked together on a table. In a 2D world, they are permanently fused. By introducing the Z-axis, we lift one ring 'up' and slide it over the other, resolving the puzzle through spatial rotation.

sections.title: The Fourth Dimension: Conceptual Projection
sections.content: Extending the logic to the 4th dimension (Tesseract). We explain that just as 3D objects cast 2D shadows, 4D objects can be understood by their 3D projections. This encourages 'Higher-Dimensional Thinking' for complex problem-solving.
sections.example: A Tesseract (Hypercube) rotating in 3D space. While we cannot 'see' the 4D object, we can solve geometry puzzles involving its structure by observing how its 3D 'shadow' changes shape as it moves.

sections.title: Summary: The Dimensional Toolkit
sections.content: A wrap-up of the two main strategies: 1. Dimensional Reduction (Unfolding/Flattening) to find paths. 2. Dimensional Expansion (Extrusion/Lifting) to bypass obstacles. Final takeaway: When stuck in a problem, ask 'Am I in the wrong dimension?'
sections.example: An animation of a character trapped in a 2D maze who suddenly grows a 3D 'jump' ability to see the exit from above and walk directly to it.
